findings.headline: Planning Development Appeals generating £124k unexpected overspend
findings.detail: Planning function is forecasting £114k net overspend driven primarily by Development Appeals costing £124k. Vacant Planning Specialist posts save £45k, but net position remains in overspend. This indicates material appeals activity or cost escalation.
findings.matters: Specific budget pressure on planning function suggests either increased appeals volume or cost per appeal rising. Indicates dispute resolution costs or increased specialist expertise required.
findings.figures: £124k Development Appeals overspend
findings.quote: Development Appeals estimated to cause a £124k overspend.

findings.headline: East of St Edmunds land acquisition faces professional fee cost overruns despite fixed purchase price
findings.detail: Council is acquiring land at East of St Edmunds (£2.25m budgeted capital project) for housing. Construction commenced May 2026. Purchase price is fixed, but 'the professional fees for the employer's agent and clerk of works may exceed the budget, although competitive quotations are being sought.' This indicates initial scoping underestimation on a major acquisition.
findings.matters: Professional fee overrun on a £2.25m capital project signals cost control issues. Even after seeking competitive quotations, fees are projected to exceed budget, suggesting inadequate initial estimation or scope creep.
findings.figures: £2.250m East of St Edmunds capital budget
findings.quote: The professional fees for the employer's agent and clerk of works may exceed the budget, although competitive quotations are being sought.

findings.headline: Vehicle maintenance overspending £137k while capital fleet replacement delayed; additional £36k income loss
findings.detail: Vehicle maintenance is forecasting £137k overspend 'until the fleet is replaced'. Separately, the council has lost £36k of expected Axis income for vehicle maintenance. The overspend persists while the capital replacement project is deferred, creating ongoing cost pressure.
findings.matters: Aging council vehicle fleet driving escalating maintenance costs. Capital replacement is deferred, suggesting budget pressure or financing constraints, while operating costs are rising as a result.
findings.figures: £137k maintenance overspend, £36k lost income
findings.quote: There is a projected overspend of vehicle maintenance of £137k until the fleet is replaced and now no more Axis income for vehicle maintenance will be received against the legacy budget of £36k.

findings.headline: Takeley housing development at risk from judicial review over community centre demolition; expenditure deferred pending legal advice
findings.detail: Takeley Development was expected to register a planning application in August 2026. However, '2026/27 expenditure could be limited subject to legal advice regarding a potential judicial review over the demolition of the community centre.' The project is budgeted at £1.250m (capital + slippage) but now faces legal uncertainty and potential delay.
findings.matters: Legal challenge creates material risk to a £1.25m capital project that is part of the council's housing delivery programme. Directly affects both capital deployment plans and the HRA's ability to service proposed new borrowing through rental income.
findings.figures: £1.250m Takeley capital budget (with slippage)
findings.quote: Expenditure in 2026/27 could be limited subject to legal advice regarding a potential judicial review over the demolition of the community centre, so will continue to be monitored.

findings.headline: HRA dwelling void properties (Alexia House, Parkside) causing £282k rent underachievement with uncertain redevelopment timeline
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account rental income is underachieving by £282k due to Alexia House and Parkside estate remaining void while awaiting redevelopment. The paper states 'plans are currently being devised' with no completion timeline. Separately, the council proposes to fund new housing delivery by borrowing against rental income (paragraph 51), creating serviceability risk if voids persist.
findings.matters: Material void housing stock represents deferred capital investment and ongoing revenue loss. Council plans to borrow for housing delivery but already has projects stalled; this affects debt serviceability assumptions.
findings.figures: £282k rent underachievement, Alexia House and Parkside awaiting redevelopment
findings.quote: This is due to the Alexia House and the Parkside estate still being void waiting for redevelopment, for which plans are currently being devised.

findings.headline: Taxi licensing income down £238k; shortfall mitigated by spending cuts and reserve draw
findings.detail: Taxi licensing income is forecast £238k below budget. The council has reduced staff and other spending by £136k and drawn an additional £43k from the licensing reserve, but still forecasts a £59k net overspend in the service. This represents a significant revenue loss in a specific income stream requiring reserve depletion to manage.
findings.matters: Material revenue loss in a discretionary service income suggests local economic headwind or demand collapse in taxi licensing. The need to draw reserves and cut spending to contain the loss indicates this is not a one-year blip.
findings.figures: £238k income loss, £136k spending reduction, £43k reserve draw, £59k net overspend
findings.quote: Taxi licensing income is down £238k but this is being mitigated by reduced salary and other expenditure of £136k and an extra £43k forecast draw down from the licensing reserve.

findings.headline: Commercial property investments of £194.4m now constrain Council's ability to take on further borrowing
findings.detail: The Council holds £194.4m in commercial property investments purchased before CIPFA's 2021 Prudential Code restricted new borrowing for investment-for-yield purposes. The paper explicitly states the Council must review "options for exiting these investments" before undertaking further borrowing. This signals these holdings are a binding constraint on debt capacity. The Council is also setting aside £0.5m annually to a commercial asset reserve, suggesting preparation for potential asset impairment.
findings.matters: For a lender, this indicates the Council's debt headroom is heavily committed to commercial property holdings that are difficult to exit, potentially limiting its ability to finance essential services or respond to financial stress.
findings.figures: £194.4m commercial investments; £85.2m additional loans to subsidiary Aspire (CRP) Ltd; £0.5m annual contribution to commercial asset reserve
findings.quote: The Council currently holds £194.4m in commercial investments primarily for financial return that were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Council will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.headline: Council explicitly exposed to interest rate risk when refinancing long-term debt
findings.detail: The Council's weighted average cost of borrowing is 3.58%, matching its investment returns, because it locked in lower rates on long-term debt in prior years while recent rate increases are reflected in shorter-term investments. The Council states: "the Council's borrowing far exceeds the balances invested, and the Council remains exposed to interest rate risk on refinancing." When current cheap borrowing matures and must be refinanced at current higher rates, the Council's costs will rise significantly.
findings.matters: This exposure means the Council faces substantial additional costs when maturing debt is refinanced at market rates, reducing financial flexibility and increasing future budget pressure during refinancing cycles.
findings.figures: Weighted average cost of borrowing 3.58%, weighted average investment return 3.58%, total borrowing £304m
findings.quote: However, the Council's borrowing far exceeds the balances invested, and the Council remains exposed to interest rate risk on refinancing.

findings.headline: Treasury investment limit breached by £37k due to timing of unconfirmed receipt
findings.detail: The Council breached its investment limit for unsecured bank deposits once during 2025/26. The breach occurred when a large unconfirmed receipt arrived after the daily external investment deadline, leaving the Council £37,000 over limit. The excess remained with its principal bankers (Barclays) and was corrected the following working day. This was the only exception to full compliance with the Treasury Management Code.
findings.matters: Even minor compliance breaches in treasury management indicate control weaknesses that matter to lenders assessing the council's financial discipline and risk management capability.
findings.figures: £37,000 over investment limit
findings.quote: The investment limit for banks (unsecured) was breached once during the year by £37k due to a large unconfirmed receipt after the daily external investment deadlines. In this case the excess amount remained with the Council's principal bankers (Barclays), and action was taken to rectify the situation on the following working day.

findings.headline: HRA borrowing policy requires new borrowing to be repayable from rental income within 40 years
findings.detail: The council has established that a key financial criterion for HRA capital investment is that any new borrowing must be repayable by the net rental stream within a 40-year period. Schemes are evaluated against this threshold, with those unable to achieve repayment marked as requiring subsidy.
findings.matters: This constraint limits the HRA's ability to borrow and indicates how disciplined the council's capital planning is; schemes that cannot service borrowing from rental income within 40 years require ongoing subsidy, which reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 40-year repayment threshold
findings.quote: One of the key financial investment criteria is to ensure that proposal meets the UDC borrowing requirement that borrowing should be repayable by the net rental stream from the scheme within a 40 year period.

findings.headline: Cabinet is approving £1.55m capital investment to convert Parkside into 14 temporary accommodation apartments
findings.detail: The council is seeking Cabinet approval to invest £1.55m in capital spending from the HRA Business Plan to upgrade and convert the vacant Parkside scheme into 14 family apartments for temporary accommodation. The investment is included within the overall HRA Business Plan due to be approved at the same Cabinet meeting.
findings.matters: This shows the scale of capital investment the council believes necessary to address temporary accommodation needs, and indicates how HRA capital resources are being deployed in response to cost pressures.
findings.figures: £1,550,000 capital investment; 14 family apartments
findings.quote: This report recommends investing £1.55m from the budgeted capital programme within the HRA Business Plan (2026 – 2056), to be approved by Cabinet in September 2026

findings.headline: Vacant Parkside site incurs approximately £64,000 annual council tax plus approximately £78,000 annual rent loss while generating no income
findings.detail: The Parkside site carries council tax liability of approximately £64,000 per year and loses rental income at approximately £1,500 per week. In addition, the council incurs ongoing costs for security, inspections and insurance while the site remains vacant.
findings.matters: Vacant HRA assets represent lost revenue and ongoing carrying costs that reduce the resources available for housing delivery and financial resilience, creating pressure to bring assets back into productive use.
findings.figures: £64,000 per year council tax; £1,500 per week rent loss (approx. £78,000 annually)
findings.quote: The Council HRA account is still liable for the payment of Council Tax in relation to the vacant Parkside scheme which amounts to just over £64,000 per year.

findings.headline: Council's net annual cost for temporary accommodation is £401,678, and this scheme is designed to reduce that cost
findings.detail: The council's gross TA spending in 2025/26 was £584,764, of which only £183,086 was recovered from government subsidy, leaving a net cost of £401,678. The council currently has 33 households in nightly paid accommodation. The paper presents the Parkside conversion as a cost-reduction strategy, bringing this provision in-house.
findings.matters: This shows structural cost pressures on the HRA that are driving capital investment decisions and indicates the HRA is spending significantly more on TA than government reimburses, which constrains financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £584,764 gross cost, £183,086 recovered, £401,678 net cost (2025/26); 33 households in nightly paid accommodation
findings.quote: The gross cost was £584,764 for the last financial year 2025/26 of which, the Council was able to recover only £183,086 in TA subsidy from the Government. Therefore, the net cost to the Council was £401,678

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Stock loss continues through Right to Buy: 17 sales in 2025/26 (spike from policy change window), with forecast normalisation
findings.detail: Right to Buy sales spiked to 17 in 2025/26 (versus 10 in 2024/25) due to a 3-week window in November 2024 before discount levels were reset to pre-2012 levels. Although RTB discounts have been reduced from 15% maximum to ~5% plus 1% per year of occupancy (capped at pre-2012 levels), the plan assumes ongoing losses through RTB. Stock has declined from 2,853 in 2012 to 2,797 at 31 March 2026 (-2% over 14 years).
findings.matters: Continuing erosion of housing stock base; RTB receipts must be reinvested to replace homes lost, competing with other investment priorities
findings.figures: RTB sales 2024/25: 10; RTB sales 2025/26: 17; stock decline 2012-2026: 2,853 to 2,797 (-56 homes, -2%)
findings.quote: The number of RTB disposals is expected to reduce in future years, following national changes to the level of discount that tenants can receive. As a result of the policy changes there were 10 sales in 2024/25 and 17 sales in 2025/26 caused by a 3-week window in November 2024

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Sheltered housing schemes (38 properties) vacant and awaiting strategic decision; options appraisal due Q2 2026/27
findings.detail: Alexia House and Parkside, totalling 38 properties, are vacant and awaiting decision about their future. An options appraisal is underway and will be reported to Members by the end of quarter two 2026-27. These are part of 11 sheltered schemes providing 397 homes for older people.
findings.matters: Asset utilisation issue; vacant stock generates no rent income but incurs carrying costs; delayed decision on future use (demolition, remodelling, or retention) locks in cost
findings.figures: 38 properties vacant (Alexia House and Parkside); total sheltered stock: 397 homes across 11 schemes
findings.quote: Two of these schemes, Alexia House and Parkside which total 38 properties, are vacant and awaiting decision about their future. An options appraisal is underway and will be reported to Members by the end of quarter two 2026-27

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Tenant satisfaction with complaints handling at 35.5% against a 44% target; performance issue in regulatory inspection context
findings.detail: Tenant Satisfaction Measure (TSM09) 'Approach to Handling Complaints' achieved only 35.5% in 2024/25 against a 44% target. This is a regulated metric under the Regulator of Social Housing's Consumer Standards inspection regime, which Uttlesford has been subject to proactively since April 2024 under a rolling 4-year inspection programme.
findings.matters: Regulatory risk; performance failure on a measured complaints handling standard during first cycle of proactive regulation; reflects on landlord's ability to meet Consumer Standards
findings.figures: TSM09 achievement: 35.5%; target: 44%; gap: -8.5 percentage points
findings.quote: TP09 Approach to Handling Complaints 44% [target] 35.5% [2024/25 result]

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Net Zero Carbon investment of £80.3m (after inflation) excluded from baseline plan because it would require continuous borrowing until year 16
findings.detail: The business plan estimates achieving Net Zero Carbon would cost £84.2m at base prices or £90.7m inflated. Since investment would not generate additional income to support borrowing costs, and would extend borrowing significantly beyond current plan, this investment is modelled only as a sensitivity. The paper notes 'this level of investment would require continued borrowing in the HRA until year 16 of the plan' and would 'remove a significant proportion of the capacity to invest in other things, such as the delivery of much needed new homes'.
findings.matters: Known material investment requirement (£80.3m net of planned activity) deferred beyond business plan; represents future funding gap or competing priority against new home delivery
findings.figures: Net Zero investment excluded: £80.3m (after allowing for planned investment); cost per dwelling: £29,900 base prices or £32,410 inflated
findings.quote: Additional investment in energy efficiency measures to achieve Net Zero Carbon, estimated at just over £80 million (after allowing for some investment included in base budgets), has currently been excluded from the baseline plan, as this level of investment would require continued borrowing in the HRA until year 16 of the plan

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Planned repairs and maintenance performance is below target across multiple metrics, including fire safety and water hygiene
findings.detail: Performance against Council Commitments and Indicators shows 'red' (below target) performance in: completion of high priority water hygiene recommendations, high priority fire safety recommendations from current and previous risk assessments, average re-let time for council homes, percentage of homes where Stock Condition Survey completed within 12 months, and percentage of emergency and non-emergency repairs completed within timescales.
findings.matters: Reactive maintenance backlog and undersized delivery capacity; regulatory compliance risk under proactive Regulator of Social Housing regime (in place since April 2024)
findings.figures: Performance reported 'red' against targets for water hygiene, fire safety, re-let times, stock condition surveys, and repair completion timescales
findings.quote: Performance was below targets set (red) in respect of the completion of high priority water hygiene recommendations and high priority fire safety recommendations from current and previous risk assessments, the average re-let time for council homes, the percentage of homes where a Stock Condition Survey has been carried out within the last 12 months, the percentage of emergency and non-emergency repairs completed within timescales

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Merger into West Essex unitary authority from April 2028 creates medium-term governance and operational execution risk
findings.detail: Uttlesford District Council will cease to exist after March 2028, merging with Epping Forest and Harlow to form West Essex unitary authority with ~18,000 homes total. The paper notes 'there will inevitably be significant challenges in the years to come in terms of how best to deliver housing services to residents in a new operating environment'. However, a new 2026-31 Housing Strategy is being developed to 'ensure that the current and future interests of Uttlesford residents are clear and follow through into the new West Essex unitary authority from 2028'.
findings.matters: Organisational continuity and service delivery risk during transition; unknown impact on HRA financial management, borrowing arrangement, or delivery of this business plan post-2028
findings.figures: West Essex unitary will comprise ~18,000 homes; Uttlesford currently holds ~2,797 homes
findings.quote: The creation of the new unitary authorities in Essex means that Uttlesford District Council will cease to exist after March 2028, and its functions will merge into the new West Essex unitary authority

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Interest Cover Ratio starts at only 1.43 in year 1, only 14% above the prudent minimum of 1.25
findings.detail: The plan adopts a 'prudent' interest cover ratio floor of 1.25 to provide a cushion against unexpected cost increases or income loss. Year 1 ICR is 1.43, rising to 1.69 by year 2. The paper notes that 'if the HRA falls below this level, careful risk management is required to ensure that the level can be returned to in future years'.
findings.matters: Limited headroom in early years if income or costs diverge from plan; early refinancing of debt at high rates creates stress on margins
findings.figures: Year 1 ICR: 1.43; Year 2: 1.69; minimum prudent threshold: 1.25; headroom in year 1: £7.883m
findings.quote: A 'prudent' interest cover ratio of 1.25 has been adopted as part of this iteration of the HRA Business Plan, recognising that if the HRA falls below this level, careful risk management is required to ensure that the level can be returned to in future years

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Material building safety and compliance costs remain unquantified: Awaab's Law, revised Decent Homes Standard, and fire safety remediation
findings.detail: Awaab's Law came into force October 2025 requiring landlords to investigate and fix damp, mould and emergency hazards within prescribed timescales. A new Decent Homes Standard (effective 2035) replaces age-based replacement with condition-based, expected to increase costs. Fire safety remediation costs are also required but not fully quantified. These are identified as future costs to be incorporated when information is available.
findings.matters: The paper explicitly states these costs are 'not currently incorporated into the business plan' pending cost quantification; they represent material contingent liabilities
findings.figures: Damp and mould quantification pending; fire and building safety compliance costs 'will need to be fully quantified'; new Decent Homes Standard costs quoted as potentially 'increased' but unquantified
findings.quote: Both of these legislative changes are anticipated to increase costs in the HRA, both in terms of capital investment in respect of the proposed new Decent Homes Standard, and in respect of responsive revenue repairs, particularly in the case of damp, condensation and mould

findings.paper_title: Appendix: Uttlesford HRA Business Plan - 2026-27 to 2055-56
findings.headline: Borrowing costs have doubled: refinancing existing debt at 6.44% versus rates of 3.01-5.07% on current loans
findings.detail: HRA debt of £78.4m matures in early years of the plan and must be refinanced. PWLB 30-year rates have risen from an average of 2.80% in September 2020 to 6.44% at the time of writing. The business plan projects peak HRA debt of £89m around year 9 as existing loans are refinanced alongside investment needs.
findings.matters: Refinancing requirement is now significantly more expensive; net new borrowing of £8.6m over 10 years is needed even after excluding home development schemes
findings.figures: HRA CFR £78.4m at 1 April 2026; existing loan rates 3.01%-5.07%; current PWLB 30-year rate 6.44%; projected peak debt £89m around year 9
findings.quote: 30-year standard maturity borrowing costs from the Public Works Loans Board were in the region of 6.44%, significantly impacting the business plan where loans are required to be re-financed or borrowing is required for additional investment

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A OPTIONS APPRAISAL OUTPUTS FOR THE PARKSIDE SITE
findings.headline: Housing Management will not support 16 one-bed units in a single scheme due to client complexity
findings.detail: For both 1-bed options delivering 16 units (whether social rent or affordable rent), Housing Management explicitly stated 'would not support the delivery of 16 1 bed flats for general needs in one scheme – complex client group', limiting viable delivery to mixed tenure schemes with smaller numbers of 1-bed units.
findings.matters: An internal operational constraint narrows delivery options and forces trade-offs between scheme size, tenure mix, and housing need, directly affecting which options the council can realistically implement.
findings.figures: 16-unit schemes rejected; alternatives require mixing 'a small number of flats with some family housing'
findings.quote: Housing Management would not support the delivery of 16 1 bed flats for general needs – complex client group.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A OPTIONS APPRAISAL OUTPUTS FOR THE PARKSIDE SITE
findings.headline: Affordable rent cap (LHA) had to be reduced and remains unaffordable for households not receiving Housing Benefit
findings.detail: The LHA rent for a 1-bed flat was reduced from £207.12 to £203 per week to meet the affordable rent ceiling. For schemes using LHA-capped rents, the document notes 'Affordability of LHA rents is high for households that are not in receipt of Housing Benefit', appearing for both 1-bed and over-60s affordable rent options, indicating occupancy and revenue risk.
findings.matters: Affordability constraints on self-payers (non-benefit recipients) reduce the addressable tenant pool and revenue sustainability, affecting scheme viability independent of initial subsidy.
findings.figures: LHA rent £203/week (reduced from £207.12)
findings.quote: The LHA rent for a 1 bed flat in Saffron Walden exceeded the 80% affordable rent cap using the average market rent for the area therefore was reduced from £207.12 to £203 per week for the purpose of the Parkside appraisal exercise... Affordability of LHA rents is high for households that are not in receipt of Housing Benefit.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A OPTIONS APPRAISAL OUTPUTS FOR THE PARKSIDE SITE
findings.headline: Scheme viability depends on uncertain Homes England grant funding that several options do not meet criteria for
findings.detail: The 4-bed social rent option explicitly notes grant funding 'would not meet Homes England VfM criteria therefore 40 year payback period would not be met unless subsidised by RTB receipts'. The temporary accommodation refurbishment 'Would not be eligible for grant funding'. The keyworker housing is 'Not likely to attract grant funding from Homes England as does not meet their strategic priorities'.
findings.matters: External grant eligibility is uncertain for schemes requiring significant subsidy, creating delivery and financial risk if RTB receipts and Homes England funding do not materialize.
findings.figures: Total scheme costs from £1,350,000 to £5,762,420; payback periods 15–40 years depending on option
findings.quote: Grant subsidy required would not meet Homes England VfM criteria therefore 40 year payback period would not be met unless subsidised by RTB receipts to reduce borrowing requirement... Would not be eligible for grant funding... Not likely to attract grant funding from Homes England as does not meet their strategic priorities

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A OPTIONS APPRAISAL OUTPUTS FOR THE PARKSIDE SITE
findings.headline: Multiple housing schemes require material unmet subsidy of £0.87m to £2.67m to meet 40-year payback periods
findings.detail: Several development options cannot achieve 40-year payback from rental income alone and require external subsidy. The new build 1-bed social rent option needs £2.67m subsidy (£245k per unit); the over-60s social rent option needs £2.23m (£93k per unit); the 1-bed affordable rent option requires £0.87m. The temporary accommodation refurbishment and general needs options ranging from £1.35m to £2.3m show subsidy needs of £1.47m for the 4-bed social rent scheme.
findings.matters: These subsidy requirements expose whether the council can finance schemes from rental income or depends on external grants and Right to Buy receipts, creating delivery risk and borrowing exposure.
findings.figures: £2,667,000 (1-bed social rent, £245K per unit), £2,232,420 (over-60s social rent, £93K per unit), £866,900 (1-bed affordable rent, £54K per unit), £1,470,000 (4-bed social rent, £245K per unit)
findings.quote: SUBSIDY REQUIRED to meet 40 year payback: £2,667,000 or £245K per unit... £2,232,420 or £93K per unit... £866,900 or £54K per unit... £1,470,000 or £245K per unit

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation in April 2028 creates medium-likelihood, high-impact risk of disruption to HRA service delivery and business planning.
findings.detail: Uttlesford is combining with Epping Forest and Harlow to form West Essex unitary authority from April 2028. The combined entity will manage approximately 18,000 HRA households. This 30-year business plan is designed to transition into the new authority, but LGR creates material execution and integration risk.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand that within 19 months the council's HRA function will merge with two others into a new entity, creating refinancing, governance, and operational continuity risks that may not be fully controllable by current management.
findings.figures: Combined HRA approximately 18,000 households; transition occurs April 2028; this plan covers 2026-2056
findings.quote: On 25 March 2026, the Government confirmed its decision to create five new unitary authorities in Essex, with Uttlesford combining with Epping Forest District Council and Harlow Council to form the new West Essex unitary authority from April 2028. The new West Essex authority will become a social landlord to approximately 18,000 households in total.

findings.headline: Significant increase in borrowing costs upon loan refinancing is identified as medium-likelihood, high-impact risk.
findings.detail: The risk register flags that when existing HRA loans mature and are refinanced, borrowing costs could increase materially. Mitigation relies on maintaining an Interest Cover Ratio floor of 1.25 and using PWLB certainty rates, but the risk remains flagged.
findings.matters: In a rising or volatile rate environment, refinancing of the £89m peak debt could materially impair HRA viability; the identified mitigation (ICR floor) may be insufficient if rates move adversely.
findings.figures: Interest Cover Ratio minimum 1.25 maintained; no cost sensitivity figures provided
findings.quote: Risk: Significant increase in borrowing costs upon loan refinancing - Likelihood: Medium, Impact: High. Mitigation: Annual review of treasury management assumptions; use of PWLB HRA/certainty rates; ICR 'golden rule' of 1.25 maintained throughout.

findings.headline: HRA Capital Financing Requirement peaks at approximately £89 million by year 9, up from £78.4 million in 2026.
findings.detail: The debt trajectory shows an initial increase of £10.6m from refinancing and development, peaking in year 9 before declining as surpluses grow. This peak debt level is material relative to a stock of 2,797 properties and represents significant refinancing exposure.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility on the full debt trajectory and the refinancing timing; the peak at year 9 creates a critical refinancing window when interest rates could have moved materially from current levels.
findings.figures: CFR £78.4m in 2026, peaking at £89m in year 9, declining thereafter; stock of 2,797 properties
findings.quote: The HRA Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) starts at £78.4 million in 2026, peaking at around £89 million by year 9 due to refinancing and development, then declining as surpluses increase and borrowing is repaid.

findings.headline: £8.6 million of net new borrowing required in the first 10 years, primarily to fund development of up to 96 new homes.
findings.detail: The Business Plan requires new HRA borrowing of £8.6m to fund development of up to 96 additional homes (23 identified, plus 73 in pipeline). The council expects rental income from these new homes to fully support the associated borrowing costs.
findings.matters: HRA debt will increase on a maturing stock; lenders assessing refinancing risk need to verify that new rental income assumptions supporting this borrowing are realistic and that development delivery does not slip, leaving debt without revenue coverage.
findings.figures: £8.6 million net new borrowing in first 10 years; up to 96 new homes (23 identified, 73 pipeline)
findings.quote: Net new borrowing of £8.6 million is required in the first 10 years, primarily to fund up to 96 new homes, with additional rental income from these homes supporting the borrowing costs.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law and Decent Homes 2 are flagged as high-likelihood cost pressures with costs still unquantified and to be incorporated in next annual update.
findings.detail: The risk register identifies these regulatory requirements as high-likelihood with medium impact. The mitigation acknowledges that additional investment costs remain to be quantified, meaning the full financial impact of these rules is not yet modelled into the business plan.
findings.matters: Future HRA financial headroom is uncertain as the full cost of mandatory regulatory compliance has not yet been quantified, creating potential for unplanned reserve drawdowns or reduced investment capacity in future years.
findings.figures: No costs specified; minimum reserves £2m identified as in-year buffer
findings.quote: Additional investment costs to be quantified and incorporated in the next annual update. Minimum reserves of £2m provide in-year buffer.

findings.headline: Decent Homes Standard 2 and net zero carbon compliance cannot be fully funded within the plan, requiring drawdown of revenue reserves.
findings.detail: The Business Plan explicitly identifies a funding shortfall to meet the new Decent Homes Standard 2 and excludes the full cost of net zero carbon achievement by 2030 due to affordability. The council plans to use revenue reserves to bridge these gaps, relying on the £2 million minimum reserve floor as a buffer.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance costs are being deferred or partially funded through reserves rather than from operations, reducing financial flexibility and indicating the council cannot absorb these costs within normal HRA operations.
findings.figures: £2 million minimum reserves maintained throughout plan; net zero carbon investment excluded from baseline; only EPC 'C' standard achievable by 2030 within baseline plan
findings.quote: The Business Plan faces a funding shortfall to fully meet the new Decent Homes Standard, requiring use of reserves, and excludes the full cost of achieving net zero carbon due to affordability constraints.

findings.headline: Council identifies business rates deficits and MTFP gaps as forward-looking financial pressures
findings.detail: The risk analysis explicitly notes that if the proposed reserve transfers are not approved, the council will struggle to manage both 'current and future business rates deficits' and 'any future MTFP gaps or HRA capital plans'. This indicates known structural pressures expected beyond 2025/26.
findings.matters: Identified forward-looking pressures on business rates income and medium-term budget sustainability are key creditworthiness indicators; they signal the council expects ongoing financial headwinds.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The Council's share of current and future business rates deficits would be harder to manage. As would any future MTFP gaps or HRA capital plans

findings.headline: HRA capital programme slipped £6.6m due to service provider underperformance, including Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund delays
findings.detail: The HRA capital outturn shows £6.557m slippage into 2026/27, including £1.824m on stock capital investment and £3.993m on the Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund. The report explicitly attributes this to service provider underperformance. These funds support the Decent Homes 2030 target, so delays jeopardize that statutory commitment.
findings.matters: Service provider contract underperformance creates execution risk; slippage against statutory housing quality targets and capital funding locked in reserves longer than planned affects HRA financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Total HRA capital slippage £6.557m from £9.119m budget; Stock capital underspend £1.824m, Social Housing Decarbonisation £3.993m
findings.quote: The HRA Capital Outturn shows slippage of £6.557m after under delivery of capital projects by the service provider.

findings.headline: Property services spending overspent by £619k, representing 56% overrun against budget
findings.detail: Property services (facilities management and common area maintenance) was budgeted at £1.101m but spent £1.720m. While other maintenance lines underspent, this concentration of cost overrun suggests material pressure, possibly from energy costs, emergency works, or service inflation.
findings.matters: Cost inflation in essential maintenance services indicates either deteriorating stock condition or market price pressures that affect future HRA sustainability and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Property services budget £1,101k, outturn £1,720k, overspend £619k
findings.quote: Property services 1,101 1,720 619

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account dwelling rents under-collected by £500k (2.7% shortfall)
findings.detail: The HRA budgeted for £18.452m in dwelling rent income but only received £17.952m, resulting in a £500k shortfall. This could indicate void properties, collection issues, or lower than expected occupancy. For an HRA that relies primarily on rent for operations, this is material.
findings.matters: Rental income is the primary revenue source for HRA operations; shortfalls directly impact the ability to fund maintenance, management, and debt service.
findings.figures: Dwelling rents budgeted (18,452) vs outturn (17,952), variance 500
findings.quote: Dwelling rents (18,452) (17,952) 500

findings.headline: Social housing decarbonation capital programme delayed due to service provider failure
findings.detail: Capital financing ran £2.954m behind budget, driven by delays to the capital programme including specifically the social housing decarbonation programme. The council attributes this to 'failure of the service provider'. It is now placing £1.286m into a Decarbonisation Fund reserve to earmark funds for future delivery.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays and contractor failure indicate project management risks; decarbonation commitments are deferred, affecting investment and potentially affected communities
findings.figures: £2.954m capital financing underspend; £1.286m transferred to Decarbonisation Fund reserve
findings.quote: The capital financing was £2.954m lower than what was budgeted due to the capital programme getting behind schedule (including the social housing decarbonation programme) with the failure of the service provider.

findings.headline: £1.1m provision made for potential HRA legal claims
findings.detail: The council has made a £1.1m provision to cover potential legal claims against the HRA. The document does not specify what these claims relate to, but the size and the fact it only emerges at outturn suggests they may be material or recent.
findings.matters: Legal claims against the HRA could affect financial resilience and may indicate compliance or service delivery issues
findings.figures: £1.1m provision
findings.quote: A provision of £1.1m has been made to cover potential HRA legal claims against the Council.

findings.headline: Void properties at Alexia and Parkside estates reduced dwelling rental income by £506k
findings.detail: HRA dwelling rental income fell short by £506k due to void properties at two named estates (Alexia and Parkside). The council says these are being addressed as part of a Housing Futures programme, but voids persisted through the full financial year.
findings.matters: HRA income stability is critical for service delivery and debt servicing; persistent voids at named estates signal lettability or management challenges
findings.figures: £506k overspend (lost income)
findings.quote: Dwelling rental income underachievement was due to void properties, including Alexia and Parkside estates, which are being addressed as part of a suite of Housing reports under the Housing Futures programme.

findings.headline: Repairs service provider failed to manage work, forcing £617k agency staff overspend and creating a maintenance backlog
findings.detail: The council's repairs service provider failed to manage work, forcing Property Services to overspend by £617k on agency staff to cover the gap. The repairs contract itself underspent by £896k due to lack of work completed, leaving a backlog. The council is putting £450k into a maintenance reserve to address this backlog next year, meaning this deferred work will become a committed cost in future budgets.
findings.matters: Service delivery failure forced unplanned costs and created a known maintenance backlog that will require future funding; this signals project management and contractor monitoring weaknesses
findings.figures: £617k overspend on Property Services; £896k contract underspend; £450k transferred to maintenance reserve
findings.quote: The costs for Property Services overspent by £617k due to the need to bring in agency staff to take on the work that a service provider was not managing.

findings.headline: Financial system (Tech One) implementation paused in June 2026 in favour of new Integra contract
findings.detail: The council was implementing Technology One as its main financial accounting system, but paused this project in June 2026 in favour of a 'more financially beneficial new contract with Integra'. This created a £86k technical overspend as the Integra licence extension had to be treated as part of the paused Tech One project until it was stopped.
findings.matters: A change of financial system mid-implementation signals either that the original decision was flawed or that circumstances changed. For a lender, system changes affect the reliability of financial reporting and need careful management to avoid control gaps or data loss.
findings.figures: £86k overspend; pause decision June 2026
findings.quote: This would be on budget and is only a technical accounting overspend because the Integra licence one year extension had to be treated as part of the Technology One accounting system implementation project until the Tech 1 project was paused in favour of a more financially beneficial new contract with Integra approved by Cabinet in June 2026.

findings.headline: Council approved and fully spent £7.6m on commercial property refurbishment through Aspire (CRP) Limited
findings.detail: The council approved £2.5m for Building 800 completion and £5.1m for Building 900 refurbishment through a commercial property entity (Aspire/CRP Limited) in August 2025, and this was fully spent in 2025-26. This represents material commercial real estate exposure outside traditional council service delivery.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council financial risk needs visibility of significant property investments and commercial exposure. A £7.6m commitment to commercial buildings signals capital strategy that may carry different risk profile than statutory service investment.
findings.figures: £2.5m for Building 800; £5.1m for Building 900; total £7.6m fully spent
findings.quote: Aspire (CRP) Limited requested an additional £2.5m to complete the Building 800 project and £5.1m for the refurbishment of Building 900, which was approved by Council in August 2025. This was fully spent.

findings.headline: Axis contract terminated due to under-performance, delaying £5.8m of housing maintenance and decarbonisation work
findings.detail: The council terminated its Axis contract with the contractor after under-performance. As a result, £1.824m of a £2.742m housing maintenance budget will slip into 2026-27, and £3.993m of a £5.1m Social Housing Decarbonisation project will also slip. Together this is 67% and 78% of their respective budgets, indicating substantial project delivery risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can deliver capital programs on time and on budget. Contractor failure affecting £5.8m of work signals project management and delivery risk, particularly in housing where decarbonisation obligations are material.
findings.figures: £1.824m of £2.742m housing maintenance budget slipped; £3.993m of £5.1m decarbonisation budget slipped
findings.quote: The termination of the Axis contract due to under-performance meant this expenditure fell behind and £1.824m of the £2.742m budget will slip into 2026/27.

findings.headline: Transport operations audit found six operational categories unsatisfactory; remediation due July 2026
findings.detail: A Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency registered auditor reviewed transport operations in March 2026 against 65 criteria. Six categories were classified as unsatisfactory, covering CO2 emissions, driver eye tests, and vehicle safety. All remedial actions are scheduled for completion by 31 July 2026.
findings.matters: Operational compliance failures in transport operations represent control weaknesses and potential licence liability. Tight remediation timelines suggest urgent issues that could affect service continuity.
findings.figures: 65 criteria examined; 6 categories rated unsatisfactory; deadline 31 July 2026
findings.quote: A Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency registered auditor undertook a review of transport operations in March 2026. The review examined 65 separate criteria and classified 6 categories as 'unsatisfactory'.

findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator gave C2 rating (below target C1), requiring improvement in tenant engagement and repairs
findings.detail: A mock inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing in 2025/26 gave a C2 rating on a scale where C1 is highest. The council is pursuing a service improvement programme with focus on tenant engagement and repairs to achieve the target C1 rating.
findings.matters: A C2 regulatory rating indicates the council is not fully meeting regulatory expectations in housing management and service delivery. This directly reflects on the quality and compliance of housing operations.
findings.figures: Rating scale C1 (highest) to C4; council achieved C2
findings.quote: The council commissioned a mock inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing during 2025/26; this inspection gave the council a 'C2' rating.

findings.headline: Information governance reporting has fallen behind due to resourcing constraints, with backlog extending into 2026/27
findings.detail: The mandatory annual Information Governance Report was not produced for 2024/25 and is scheduled for 2026/27 'resources permitting'. This creates a compliance gap in mandatory reporting on data protection, information governance, data breaches, and Freedom of Information performance.
findings.matters: Information governance is a statutory reporting requirement. Persistent resourcing gaps preventing compliance reports suggest staff constraints and inability to adequately manage data protection and compliance risks.
findings.figures: Reports delayed: 2024/25 not produced; 2025/26 deferred to 2026/27
findings.quote: No report was produced for 24/25 due to resourcing issues. The 25/26 outturn position will be presented to Committee during the 26/27 year, again resources permitting.

findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion is moderate, not substantial, indicating control weaknesses persist
findings.detail: Internal Audit raised the annual opinion from 'limited' in the prior year to 'moderate' in 2025/26, based on 11 completed audits: 2 rated substantial, 5 moderate, 3 limited, and 1 with no assurance. While 90 historic recommendations were closed, the ongoing mix of audit ratings shows control issues remain.
findings.matters: A moderate audit opinion means the council's internal controls are not fully robust. Lenders require substantial or unqualified audit opinions as evidence of financial control effectiveness.
findings.figures: 11 internal audits completed: 2 substantial, 5 moderate, 3 limited, 1 no assurance; 90 prior-year recommendations closed
findings.quote: Internal Audit considers that corporate governance, risk management and internal control processes have improved in 2025/26, sufficiently to raise the overall opinion from 'limited' to 'moderate'.

findings.headline: Housing maintenance service failed to external contractor and was replaced with in-house provision within 12 months
findings.detail: The council ended its joint venture with Norse Group (UNSL) on 31 March 2025 and contracted with Axis Europe from 1 April 2025. However, Axis encountered 'operational, performance, and delivery challenges' that led to early termination. The council then implemented an in-house maintenance service from 1 April 2026. This represents two major service model changes in 12 months and suggests either unexpected costs or service quality issues from the contracted provider.
findings.matters: Service delivery disruption and rapid strategy reversal indicate procurement or contract management issues that could result in unexpected financial exposure and operational risk to housing services.
findings.figures: Three transitions in 12 months: UNSL ceased 31 March 2025; Axis Europe from 1 April 2025; in-house from 1 April 2026
findings.quote: Following the mobilisation of the Axis contract, we encountered several operational, performance, and delivery challenges. These issues ultimately led to the early cessation of the contract and the decision to implement an In-House Maintenance Service, which went live on 1 April 2026.

findings.headline: Commercial portfolio valuation has declined against purchase price; Skyway House lost £5.5m and Amazon lost £6.75m since acquisition
findings.detail: Asset valuations as at 30 September 2025 show material declines. Skyway House (paid £20m, valued £14.5m), Amazon Gloucester (paid £42.7m, valued £35.95m), and others show similar patterns. The non-CRP portfolio shows £186.8m cost against £169.65m valuation (9% loss overall). Only the disputed Aspire valuation at £110.35m supports the total portfolio claim of £280m.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the trend in asset values and whether further decline is expected; this affects the security available against the £238.6m borrowing position
findings.figures: Portfolio cost £275.6m valued at £280m; non-CRP assets £186.8m cost vs £169.65m valuation; individual declines: Skyway £5.5m, Amazon £6.75m, others material
findings.quote: Whilst asset values have declined, the rental income has increased through rent reviews.

findings.headline: Council is committing £68.6m to Chesterford Research Park expansion through 2031 despite rule constraints and inability to exit
findings.detail: Despite being unable to sell the 50% stake and facing a changed regulatory environment, the council is committed to major capital at the park: £40m for new buildings, £5.1m for refurbishment, £13.5m for end-of-lease refurbishment by 2031. Para 22 forecasts annual contributions of £4-12.6m. No payment is due on the largest loans until April 2026-2027, creating a cliff.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether the council can sustain this level of capital commitment given stated budget shortfalls; construction cost inflation or tenant issues could force additional unplanned borrowing
findings.figures: £68.6m total: New Building 1 £40m, Building 500 £10m, Building 900 refurbishment £5.1m, other lease-end refurbishment £13.5m
findings.quote: The joint venture 5 year business plan for Chesterford Research Park sets out ambitions for two new builds as well as specific refurbishment of Building 900. Over the lifetime of the plan there will also be a number of other units reaching end of lease and requiring refurbishment, accordingly a contribution of £1,500,000 has been built into the 2026/27 financial year and £3,000,000 each year thereafter.

findings.headline: CIPFA rule changes force the council to hold all assets long-term instead of the planned sell-and-refresh strategy
findings.detail: The original plan was to sell assets after holding them, reinvest proceeds, and avoid asset aging. This is no longer possible: para 39 states 'It will not now be possible to sell assets and buy new, the council will need to retain some or all of the assets for the longer term.' This lock-in increases refurbishment risk as assets age through lease cycles.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know the portfolio is becoming progressively older with rising end-of-lease costs; the council is building a £500k annual reserve but holds only £6m total against £275.6m in assets
findings.figures: £275.6m portfolio; £6m Commercial Asset Reserve at end 2025/26; £500k annual contributions; major refurbishment costs forecast £1.5m-£3m annually from 2027
findings.quote: It will not now be possible to sell assets and buy new, the council will need to retain some or all of the assets for the longer term.

findings.headline: Attempted sale of Chesterford Research Park shareholding attracted interest but no acceptable bid, leaving £88.8m committed to a held asset
findings.detail: In February 2024 the council agreed to market its 50% stake in Chesterford Research Park. Despite significant interest, no acceptable bid was received. The council continues to commit major capital: £68.6m is planned for 2026-2031, with no ability to exit. The asset cannot be sold quickly to meet liquidity needs.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess the council's actual liquidity position; failure to achieve a sale despite marketing suggests the largest single asset may be harder to realise than expected
findings.figures: 50% share valued at £110.35m; £88.8m in existing loans to subsidiary; £68.6m further investment planned
findings.quote: In February 2024 Council agreed to market, through its wholly owned subsidiary Aspire (CRP) Limited, the 50% share in Chesterford Research Park. Whilst significant interest was shown in the sale process no acceptable bid has to date been received.

findings.headline: The 2026-2031 MTFP contains significant and rising shortfalls which the commercial portfolio can no longer fully offset
findings.detail: The council's original strategy, approved in 2020, was to use commercial property income to cover government funding reductions via a £300m investment fund. Changes to the CIPFA Prudential Code 2021 and MRP rules mean this will no longer work. The council now has no mitigation for forecast shortfalls beyond asset sales, which are discretionary.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's main strategy for bridging budget gaps is no longer viable and there is no named alternative plan
findings.figures: £300m allocation approved; £275.6m deployed; generating £14.8m-£17.7m annual rental income over next five years
findings.quote: the 2026 - 2031 MTFP has significant and rising shortfalls which cannot be fully offset by the income form the commercial portfolio

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX I - UDC PROPOSED 5% REVENUE SAVINGS 2026.27
findings.headline: Health Improvement Grant savings depend on external funding that is not guaranteed
findings.detail: The council proposes a £4k saving in the Health Improvement team budget, intending to 'top up the £4K with the Essex Funding.' However, the document explicitly states: 'The risk is whether this funding pot remains in the future.' This is external funding over which the council has no control.
findings.matters: The council's budget for this service area is now dependent on a funding stream it does not control. If Essex funding is withdrawn, the council faces a pressure it has already assumed away.
findings.figures: £4,000 assumed saving from budget reduction; contingent on continued Essex Funding
findings.quote: There is a ring-fenced health improvement grant from ECC and we are accountable how we spend this. Also we are not sure what we will get next year. So there is the potential to reduce the team budget by £4K and top up the £4K with the Essex Funding. The risk is whether this funding pot remains in the future.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX I - UDC PROPOSED 5% REVENUE SAVINGS 2026.27
findings.headline: Finance Service training budget cut could create capacity risk if accountant turnover occurs
findings.detail: The council is reducing the finance service training budget by £3.5k and eliminating one of two trainee accountant posts. The document explicitly flags the risk: 'If a current Accountant left and we needed to hire a part qualified replacement with training needs, this would result in a budget pressure.' This suggests the council recognizes its finance function is now at reduced capacity.
findings.matters: A lender depends on the council having finance staff capacity to manage accounts and reporting. Reduced training budget and fewer trainees limits the team's ability to absorb turnover or skill gaps.
findings.figures: £3,500 training reduction; £8,200 professional subscriptions reduction; reduction from 2 trainees to 1
findings.quote: If a current Accountant left and we needed to hire a part qualified replacement with training needs, this would result in a budget pressure.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX I - UDC PROPOSED 5% REVENUE SAVINGS 2026.27
findings.headline: Original £1.96m savings target only 64% achieved; £700k pushed to 2027/28
findings.detail: The council identified £1.96m in savings targets across all services but allocated only £1.26m to 2026/27, deferring £700k to the following year. Large service areas show zero agreed savings despite targets: Environment (£72.6k target, £0 agreed), Grounds Maintenance (£23.2k target, £0), Street Cleansing (£28.2k), Street Services (£16.6k), Homelessness (£25.1k flagged as 'not possible, see growth bid'), Housing Strategy (£3.4k flagged as 'cannot be reduced').
findings.matters: The council could not find savings it identified as needed, indicating service areas it considers essential or challenging to cut. This suggests budget pressure on those services going forward.
findings.figures: £1,960,430 target; £1,260,430 allocated 2026/27; £700,000 deferred to 2027/28; shortfall of £699,784 (35.7% of target unachieved)
findings.quote: TOTAL SAVINGS IDENTIFIED 1,960,430 / Allocated to 2027/28 700,000 / TOTAL SAVINGS ALLOCATED TO 2026/27 1,536,974 1,260,430

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX I - UDC PROPOSED 5% REVENUE SAVINGS 2026.27
findings.headline: Dunmow Depot sale of £83,750 is conditional on planning permission being granted
findings.detail: The council is claiming £83,750 in savings from disposal of the New Street Depot. This saving is explicitly conditional: 'Sale is subject to planning permission and planning application has been submitted.' If planning is refused, this saving does not happen.
findings.matters: This is an assumed asset realization with material uncertainty. A lender would need to know whether the 2026/27 budget can be met if planning permission is refused.
findings.figures: £83,750 assumed saving; contingent on planning approval
findings.quote: Following sale of New Street Depot. Sale is subject to planning permission and planning application has been submitted.

findings.headline: Contingency budget at 9.9% of funding (£1.735m) due to Blueprint and LGR execution risks
findings.detail: The council's contingency budget is unusually high at 9.9% of total funding. Without Blueprint 2.0 and LGR risks, it would normally be 5.7%. The council is explicitly flagging £500k contingency for Blueprint delivery risk and £250k for LGR cost risk. This high contingency is a material call on the budget if risks crystallise.
findings.matters: High contingency indicates management's lack of confidence in achieving budget targets. If contingency is drawn, the budget deficit worsens immediately.
findings.figures: Total contingency £1.735m (9.9% of funding); Blueprint risk £500k; LGR risk £250k; normal contingency would be 5.7%
findings.quote: The total contingency represents 9.9% of the council's funding, which may seem high, but Blueprint 2.0 and in particular LGR are large risky projects.

findings.headline: HRA transitioning to in-house delivery model (IHDM); significant execution risk on maintenance and repairs
findings.detail: The council is moving HRA maintenance and repairs from external contracts (Axis and UNSL) to in-house delivery model. The budget includes £1.273m additional spend to embed IHDM, deal with legacy issues from the Axis and UNSL contracts, and address new social housing regulations. The council acknowledges: 'There is a risk that the costs to deliver a basic quality of service will be greater than expected or that the transition will not be as smooth, leading to additional costs.'
findings.matters: Contract transitions are high-risk operational changes. Failure to execute efficiently could result in higher-than-budgeted costs or service quality issues in the council's social housing stock.
findings.figures: HRA maintenance and repairs budget increase £1.273m to embed IHDM; new staffing posts created (Insight Officer, Damp/Mould Officer, Complaints Officer)
findings.quote: There is a risk that the costs to deliver a basic quality of service will be greater than expected or that the transition will not be as smooth, leading to additional costs.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant at risk of £278k reduction; future funding uncertain
findings.detail: DEFRA allocated £1.175m EPR grant for 2026/27, which is £278k less than 2025/26. From 2026/27, this grant must be allocated directly to Refuse and Recycling services to demonstrate use, rather than sitting in general funding. 'The Government has not confirmed this full amount will be maintained, so is a risk for years beyond 2026/27.' Waste and recycling is listed as a high-risk budget area due to market volatility.
findings.matters: EPR funding is not stable. A further reduction would materially impact waste services, which are already subject to fuel and disposal cost volatility.
findings.figures: EPR allocation 2026/27 £1.175m (down £278k from 2025/26); market volatility risk rated High on impact and probability
findings.quote: The Government has not confirmed this full amount will be maintained, so is a risk for years beyond 2026/27.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit Subsidy gap growing £200k per year; Homelessness Prevention Grant severely restricted
findings.detail: The council faces a structural pressure in temporary accommodation: it pays housing benefit to private landlords but receives only a partial government subsidy, creating an annual £200k gap that is growing. From 2026/27, the government's Homelessness Prevention Grant can only be spent 30% on staff salaries, making it much harder to resource homelessness services. The council has put aside additional contingency but notes 'there is no certainty that this is sufficient.'
findings.matters: This is a demand-driven, structural cost that the council cannot control. It will continue to grow as housing costs rise and homelessness increases.
findings.figures: Housing Benefit Subsidy gap growth £200k per year; Homelessness Prevention Grant now 30% for salaries only (down from no restriction)
findings.quote: Housing benefit subsidy gap is growing faster than expected. There is a contingency in Corporate Items but there is no certainty that this is sufficient.

findings.headline: Interest rate exposure of £106m; financing costs consume 75% of net revenue stream
findings.detail: The council holds £106m of short-term borrowing exposed to interest rate movements. Every 0.25% interest rate move costs £250k annually. The Bank of England base rate was cut from 4.0% to 3.75% in December 2025, but the council's treasury advisors forecast rates will stay at 3.25% from mid-2026. Prudential indicator shows financing costs represent 75% of the council's net revenue stream in 2026/27, the highest on record.
findings.matters: Interest rate risk is material and rising. The council's financial sustainability is increasingly dependent on interest rate movements outside its control. High financing costs ratio indicates limited headroom.
findings.figures: £106m short-term borrowing exposure; £250k per 0.25% rate move annually; financing costs 75% of net revenue stream 2026/27
findings.quote: The council is exposed to short-term interest rates to the tune of £106m. Every 0.25% movement in interest rates on £100m is a £250k impact on the council's bottom line over the period of a year.

findings.headline: Commercial property income represents 99% of net revenue stream in 2026/27; Aspire (CRP) is currently up for sale
findings.detail: Investment properties contribute £722k to the 2026/27 budget, mainly from Aspire (CRP) Limited loans and rents from Chesterford Research Park (50% council-owned). The prudential indicator shows net income from commercial investments is 99% of the net revenue stream in 2026/27. However, the document states Aspire 'is currently up for sale'. Loss of this asset would eliminate this income stream and force a major budget rebalancing.
findings.matters: The council is heavily dependent on a single commercial asset that is actively for sale. This represents both immediate income risk and uncertainty about the council's financial position if a sale completes.
findings.figures: Investment Property contribution 2026/27 £722k; commercial income 99% of net revenue stream; borrowing to Aspire £281.4m (Commercial Investments CFR)
findings.quote: subject to the council retaining Aspire (CRP) Limited, as is assumed in the MTFP, although it is currently up for sale.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates £2m-£3.75m budget uncertainty; council merges 1 April 2028
findings.detail: Uttlesford is merging into a new unitary council on 1 April 2028, creating profound uncertainty over costs, service integration, and future funding levels. The council has set aside £750k over 3 years (2025/26-2027/28) plus a new £2m LGR reserve. However, 'it is difficult to budget for LGR. The council has an annual budget but these are by no means spec'd out and unexpected costs could easily arise.' The contingency budget includes £250k for LGR risk.
findings.matters: LGR is a fundamental structural change affecting the council's viability beyond 2028. Lenders need confidence in the merged entity's financial sustainability and the transition costs.
findings.figures: £750k LGR budget over 3 years; £2m LGR reserve created; £250k contingency for LGR risk; merger date 1 April 2028
findings.quote: It is difficult to budget for LGR. The council has an annual budget but these are by no means spec'd out and unexpected costs could easily arise, whence this sum of money would be called upon.

findings.headline: Blueprint 2.0 savings programme has not identified £6.214m of the £10.024m target needed by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's Blueprint 2.0 savings programme is critical to managing the FFR impact. Of the £10.024m target across the MTFP, only £2.257m has been applied to 2026/27 and £2.051m identified. This leaves £6.214m 'still to be identified leading into 2028/29'. The council acknowledges: 'Blueprint 2.0 hasn't identified sufficient savings for the final two years as yet. This will need to form part of LGR discussions with merger partners.'
findings.matters: If these savings are not delivered, the council's deficits are understated and reserve depletion accelerates. This is a material execution risk.
findings.figures: Total Blueprint target £10.024m; identified to date £2.257m + £2.051m = £4.308m; gap £6.214m (62%); £8.265m cumulative unallocated by 2030/31
findings.quote: Blueprint 2.0 hasn't identified sufficient savings for the final two years as yet. This will need to form part of LGR discussions with merger partners once known

findings.headline: Usable reserves will be depleted by end of MTFP period; deficits run throughout 5-year plan
findings.detail: The council explicitly states 'usable reserves are all but depleted by the end of the MTFP period' and forecasts cumulative drawdown of reserves of £6.984m by 2030/31. General Fund reserves decline from £23.402m to £17.430m, with further deterioration if Blueprint savings targets are not met. Deficits are planned for every year: £1.630m (2026/27), rising to £2.091m (2029/30).
findings.matters: The council is using reserves to fund current operations, not capital investment. This is unsustainable and a red flag for lending capacity. Reserve depletion reduces financial resilience.
findings.figures: Cumulative reserve drawdown £6.984m over MTFP; General Fund reserve C/fwd 2030/31 £17.430m (down from £23.402m); annual deficits £1.630m, £1.799m, £610m, £2.091m
findings.quote: usable reserves are all but depleted by the end of the MTFP period and, subject to LGR, significant further savings need to be identified in the last years of the current MTFP.

findings.headline: One-year Adjustment Support Grant masks underlying deficit; full FFR impact hits from 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: The government provided a one-year matching grant of £1.015m to soften FFR impact in 2026/27, but the council assumes this is 'one-year only'. After 2026/27, the full FFR reduction hits unmitigated. Transitional protection also expires after year 3, creating a material funding cliff. Revenue Support Grant collapses from £6.165m in 2026/27 to £2.205m by 2030/31 (64% cut).
findings.matters: The current budget masks a structural deficit. Lenders need to understand the council's plans for years 2-5, when this grant disappears and funding falls dramatically.
findings.figures: RSG falls from £6,165k (2026/27) to £2,205k (2030/31); Adjustment Support Grant £1,015k for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The Government has mitigated the impact of the reduction in 2026/27 by way of a matching 'Adjustment Support Grant'. At the present time the indications are that this is a one-year only grant and for the purposes of this budget that assumption applies.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review cuts Uttlesford's funding by 4-5% and the council is in the top 20 worst-affected districts
findings.detail: The government's FFR formula change announced 9 February 2026 reduced Uttlesford's funding by a further £1.015 million annually. Compared to 2024/25, funding falls 4%; compared to 2025/26, it falls 5%. The council notes this 'has particularly hit UDC badly' and Uttlesford appears in the Rural Services Network's top 20 percentile of councils worst affected by FFR.
findings.matters: This is a permanent structural reduction in grant funding, not a temporary pressure. It directly affects the council's revenue base and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £1.015m annual reduction (announced 9 February 2026); 4-5% funding reduction versus prior years
findings.quote: This has particularly hit UDC badly as this has led to a reduction in funding of 4% when compared to 2024/25 and 5% when compared to 2025/26

findings.headline: Council must retain PWLB access by declaring commercial investments are not primarily for yield, creating potential tension with capital strategy
findings.detail: New PWLB rules restrict lending to councils buying investment assets primarily for yield. The council explicitly states it will avoid this activity to maintain PWLB access. However, commercial investments make up the majority of the capital programme (£266-314m of £361-419m CFR), creating potential policy constraint.
findings.matters: Loss of PWLB access would force the council to seek more expensive alternative borrowing sources, directly increasing interest costs and reducing affordability
findings.figures: Commercial investments as % of CFR: 74% (2025) → 75% (2029); Current PWLB borrowing: £207m of £294.5m total (70%)
findings.quote: PWLB loans are no longer available to local authorities planning to buy investment assets primarily for yield; the Council intends to avoid this activity in order to retain its access to PWLB loans.

findings.headline: Capital programme requires £378m borrowing over five years, predominantly for commercial investments
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement grows from £361m to £419m over the forecast period, driven by capital expenditure that is heavily weighted to commercial investments (£266-314m) rather than core services. The council must borrow £378m in total over the forecast period to fund this.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess the returns on commercial investments and whether the capital programme is sustainable, and whether commercial asset valuations are stable
findings.figures: CFR: £361m (2025) → £419m (2029); Commercial investments within CFR: £266m (2025) → £314m (2029); Total borrowing requirement: £378m over forecast period
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme, but minimal investments and will therefore be required to borrow up to £378m over the forecast period.

findings.headline: Pension actuarial controls ineffective for second consecutive year; £2.15m minimum funding liability applied
findings.detail: Controls for reviewing the council's defined benefit pension valuation are ineffective for the second year running. Management's review is insufficiently detailed and documented to be relied upon. As a result, a minimum funding liability of £2,150k has been applied to restrict the net pension surplus to nil, reflecting that the surplus cannot be recovered given future service costs and minimum funding requirements.
findings.matters: The pension scheme represents material liabilities (£82.1m) and assets (£119.9m). Without effective review controls on actuarial assumptions, pension valuations could be materially wrong. A persistent, unresolved control weakness (second year) indicates governance risk.
findings.figures: Defined benefit asset £119.9m (up £5.4m YoY); defined benefit liability £82.1m (up £9.3m YoY); minimum funding liability £2,150k
findings.quote: Actuarial assumptions are assessed by management for appropriateness. However, the review was not performed on a sufficiently detailed or documented basis to allow us to rely on the control. Consequently, we concluded that controls in place to review the valuation were ineffective, consistent with the prior period.

findings.headline: Segregation of duties control failure in journal posting system due to General Ledger limitations
findings.detail: The auditor identified a control deficiency in the automated segregation of duties for posting journal transactions. This deficiency arises from limitations in the council's General Ledger system itself, not from process failures. While testing of high-risk journals found no unsupported entries, the underlying control weakness creates an ongoing fraud risk.
findings.matters: Segregation of duties is a foundational control against fraudulent or erroneous transactions. A weakness here increases the risk that management override, unauthorized transactions, or errors could be recorded in the financial statements without detection.
findings.figures: 8 high-risk journal entries examined
findings.quote: We have identified a control deficiency regarding the enforcement of automated segregation of duties in posting of journal transactions due to the limitations of the General Ledger system.

findings.headline: Control deficiencies identified in management review of £590m+ property and investment assets
findings.detail: The auditor has identified control deficiencies in management's review processes for Council Dwellings (£375.8m), Other Land and Buildings (£45.6m), and Investment Property (£170.2m). In each case, management lacks a formal, documented review process for the valuation reports produced by external valuers. This represents a significant gap in internal controls over assets totalling over £590m.
findings.matters: Property and investment assets represent the majority of the council's balance sheet and collateral position. Without formal management review controls, there is elevated risk that valuations could be materially wrong without detection, affecting reported net worth and borrowing covenant compliance.
findings.figures: Council Dwellings £375.8m (£3.9m increase YoY); Other Land & Buildings £45.6m (£1m decrease YoY); Investment Property £170.2m (£3.9m increase YoY); total £590.6m
findings.quote: We evaluated the design and implementation of controls in place for management to review the valuation and the appropriateness of assumptions used and have raised a control deficiency around the lack of formal review of the valuation report.

findings.headline: No audit assurance over usable reserves since 2019-20 due to legacy audit backlog
findings.detail: The auditor states there is no assurance over the level of usable reserves for the six years from 2019-20 onwards. This is a material gap because councils face statutory duty to balance their annual budget, and when they do not, financial pressures fall on usable reserves and constrain the following year's budget. Without verified opening reserves position, it is impossible to assess the council's true financial position or borrowing capacity.
findings.matters: Usable reserves are the only resources a council can freely spend. Without verified reserves since 2019-20, a lender cannot determine available headroom, the council's resilience to cost pressures, or its actual borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: 2019-20 onwards (six financial years)
findings.quote: There is no assurance provided over the level of usable reserves for 2019-20 onwards, therefore there is a risk relating to the accuracy of the opening level of reserves available to the Council to support cost pressures.

findings.headline: Auditors issuing disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements due to inability to verify reserves split before statutory backstop date
findings.detail: KPMG cannot obtain sufficient audit evidence over the split of usable and unusable reserves at 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2024 before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026. The auditor views this inability as 'pervasive to the Council's and the Group's financial position' and is therefore disclaiming their opinion on the entire 2024/25 financial statements.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the council's financial position cannot be independently verified. Lenders cannot reliably assess the council's net worth, solvency, or reserves available to support borrowing and spending commitments.
findings.figures: Statutory backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: we have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the Council's and the Group's financial position
